subtopics.name: Care of clients with sensory impairment

questions.stem: A client with schizophrenia started IV haloperidol 3 days ago for severe agitation. The client is now confused and mute, with rigid arms that resist movement evenly through the full range. Temperature is 40.1 °C (104.2 °F), heart rate 128/min, blood pressure swinging between 168/100 and 98/60 mm Hg, and the skin is drenched in sweat. Creatine kinase is 18,400 units/L. Complete the diagram by placing the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor.

actions.text: Stop the haloperidol and notify the provider
Start cooling measures and give IV fluids as prescribed
Give another dose of haloperidol to control the confusion
Add a second antipsychotic such as olanzapine at a low dose
Encourage the client to walk to loosen the rigid muscles

parameters.text: Mood and thought content each shift
Weight compared with the admission weight

rationale.correct: NMS: hyperthermia, lead-pipe rigidity, altered mental status, autonomic instability and high CK after antipsychotics. Stop the drug, cool, hydrate, and monitor temperature, urine output and CK.

perOption.c1: High fever, lead-pipe rigidity, confusion, unstable blood pressure and a very high CK days after starting an antipsychotic are neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
perOption.c2: Serotonin syndrome follows serotonergic drugs and causes clonus and hyperreflexia, not lead-pipe rigidity.
perOption.c3: Dystonia causes sudden muscle spasms without fever or autonomic instability.
perOption.c4: Catatonia can look similar, but fever, autonomic instability and a very high CK after haloperidol point to NMS.
perOption.a1: Stopping the antipsychotic is the first treatment.
perOption.a2: Cooling treats hyperthermia, and fluids protect the kidneys from muscle breakdown products.
perOption.a4: Any antipsychotic can worsen the syndrome.
perOption.a5: Activity adds heat and the rigid, confused client may fall.
perOption.p1: Shows whether cooling and treatment are working.
perOption.p2: Rhabdomyolysis can cause acute kidney injury; urine output and CK show the risk.
perOption.p3: Psychiatric symptoms are followed later; they do not guide the emergency.
perOption.p4: Weight does not reflect the acute course of NMS.
perOption.p5: Bowel function is not a guide to NMS treatment.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: Five minutes after an IV infusion of cefazolin begins, a client says their throat feels tight. The nurse hears wheezing in both lungs and sees hives spreading across the chest. Blood pressure is 78/42 mm Hg (it was 126/80), heart rate is 132/min and SpO2 is 88%. Complete the diagram by placing the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor.

actions.text: Stop the infusion and give IM epinephrine as prescribed
Call the rapid response team and give high-flow oxygen
Give oral diphenhydramine and recheck in 30 minutes
Slow the infusion to half the rate and keep watching
Raise the head of the bed to 90 degrees with the legs down

rationale.correct: Anaphylaxis: stop the trigger, give IM epinephrine, support the airway with oxygen, give IV fluids and monitor vital signs and breathing; reactions can recur hours later.

perOption.c1: Throat tightness, wheezing, hives and hypotension minutes after a drug is started is anaphylaxis.
perOption.c2: That reaction follows rapid vancomycin and causes flushing without hypotension and wheezing.
perOption.c3: Asthma causes wheezing but not hives and shock right after a drug starts.
perOption.c4: Vasovagal reactions cause a slow heart rate and no hives or wheezing.
perOption.a1: Stopping the drug and giving IM epinephrine in the thigh is first-line treatment.
perOption.a2: Airway and breathing support and help are needed at once.
perOption.a3: Antihistamines are add-on treatment; they do not reverse shock or airway swelling.
perOption.a4: Any further drug worsens the reaction.
perOption.a5: Sitting up worsens hypotension; the client is laid flat with legs raised unless breathing requires otherwise.
perOption.p1: Show whether shock is responding to epinephrine and fluids.
perOption.p2: Show whether airway swelling and bronchospasm are improving.
perOption.p3: Glucose is not a guide to anaphylaxis treatment.
perOption.p4: Temperature is not a key guide to anaphylaxis.
perOption.p5: Bowel sounds do not guide treatment.

questions.stem: A client in cardiogenic shock who weighs 70 kg is prescribed dopamine at 5 mcg/kg/min by continuous IV infusion. The pharmacy sends dopamine 400 mg in 250 mL of 5% dextrose in water. The nurse is programming a pump that is set up in mL/hr and has no drug library entry for this concentration. At what rate should the nurse set the pump? Round to one decimal place.

rationale.correct: Dose: 5 mcg x 70 kg = 350 mcg/min x 60 = 21,000 mcg/hr = 21 mg/hr. Concentration: 400 mg / 250 mL = 1.6 mg/mL. Rate: 21 / 1.6 = 13.125, which rounds to 13.1 mL/hr.

questions.stem: A client with a traumatic brain injury and signs of rising intracranial pressure is on the neurosurgical unit. The nurse checks the IV fluids prescribed for maintenance. Which fluid should the nurse question?

options.text: 0.9% sodium chloride at 75 mL/hr
5% dextrose in water at 75 mL/hr
Lactated Ringer's solution at 75 mL/hr
3% sodium chloride as a slow infusion as prescribed

rationale.correct: Avoid hypotonic fluids, including D5W, in clients with brain injury or raised ICP because they increase cerebral edema.

perOption.a: Isotonic saline is commonly used after brain injury because it does not shift water into brain cells.
perOption.b: D5W acts as a hypotonic fluid once the glucose is used, moving water into brain cells and worsening cerebral edema.
perOption.c: Lactated Ringer's is close to isotonic and less likely to worsen swelling than D5W.
perOption.d: Hypertonic saline is sometimes used to reduce intracranial pressure.

questions.stem: A client receiving total parenteral nutrition through a central line has fingerstick glucose readings of 248, 262 and 285 mg/dL over the last 12 hours. The client has no history of diabetes. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Stop the TPN infusion until the glucose falls below 200 mg/dL, then restart it at the same rate
Report the readings to the provider, expecting insulin to be added or the rate adjusted
Slow the TPN to half the rate without telling the provider to bring the glucose down
Recheck the glucose with a lab blood draw tomorrow morning before taking further action

rationale.correct: High glucose is common with TPN; report it, and expect insulin coverage or formula changes. Never stop TPN suddenly.

perOption.a: Stopping TPN suddenly can cause rebound hypoglycemia.
perOption.b: Hyperglycemia is a common TPN complication; it is managed with insulin or by changing the formula.
perOption.c: The nurse does not change the TPN rate without a prescription.
perOption.d: Rising glucose needs prompt reporting, not a wait until tomorrow.

questions.stem: A client with gout starts allopurinol 100 mg daily. Which statement shows the client understands the teaching?

options.text: "I'll take it when a flare starts, to stop the pain in my big toe."
"I'll drink at least 2 to 3 L of fluid a day while taking it."
"I'll eat more organ meats and shellfish to keep my protein up."
"I'll stop the medicine if I get a rash, but I won't need to tell anyone."

rationale.correct: Allopurinol is taken daily to prevent gout; drink plenty of fluids, limit purines and alcohol and report any rash at once.

perOption.a: Allopurinol prevents attacks by lowering uric acid and is taken every day; it does not treat an acute flare.
perOption.b: High fluid intake helps prevent uric acid kidney stones.
perOption.c: Organ meats and shellfish are high in purines and raise uric acid.
perOption.d: A rash can be the first sign of a serious reaction and must be reported right away.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: A client with chronic kidney disease receives epoetin alfa weekly. Today the hemoglobin is 12.4 g/dL (it was 10.8 a month ago), and the blood pressure is 168/98 mm Hg. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Give the dose, since the higher hemoglobin shows the drug is working well
Hold the dose and report the hemoglobin and blood pressure to the provider
Give the dose and recheck the blood pressure in 1 hour to see whether it has settled down
Double the dose next week to keep the hemoglobin from falling again

rationale.correct: Erythropoiesis-stimulating agents raise the risk of hypertension, stroke and clots; hold them when hemoglobin exceeds the target or blood pressure is uncontrolled.

perOption.a: A hemoglobin above the target with uncontrolled blood pressure raises the risk of stroke and clots.
perOption.b: Doses are held or lowered when hemoglobin goes above about 11 g/dL and when blood pressure is uncontrolled.
perOption.c: Giving the dose adds to the risk; it should be held first.
perOption.d: This would raise the hemoglobin further and add risk.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: A 74-year-old client with a new hip fracture has never taken opioids. The provider prescribes a fentanyl 50 mcg/hr transdermal patch for acute pain. Why should the nurse question this prescription?

options.text: Fentanyl patches take 12 to 24 hours to reach full effect and are not for opioid-naive clients
Fentanyl patches cannot be used in older adults because they cause skin breakdown
The patch has to be changed at 8-hour intervals, which is hard to manage on a busy unit with many clients
Fentanyl is a weak opioid that will not be strong enough to control the pain of a hip fracture

rationale.correct: Transdermal fentanyl is not for opioid-naive clients or acute pain; it is slow to start and slow to wear off, and can cause life-threatening respiratory depression.

perOption.a: Transdermal fentanyl is for opioid-tolerant clients with stable, chronic pain; in opioid-naive clients it can cause fatal respiratory depression.
perOption.b: Skin irritation can occur, but it is not the main reason to question this prescription.
perOption.c: Patches are usually changed every 72 hours.
perOption.d: Fentanyl is a potent opioid, about 50 to 100 times stronger than morphine.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: A client is being discharged on apixaban for atrial fibrillation. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Take the doses at about the same times each day and do not skip doses
Have your INR blood test checked once a week at the anticoagulation clinic
Tell your dentist and other providers that you take an anticoagulant
Report black stools, blood in the urine or unusual bruising
Avoid eating green leafy vegetables such as spinach and kale while taking this drug
Use ibuprofen rather than acetaminophen for minor pain

rationale.correct: Direct oral anticoagulants: take on schedule, report bleeding, tell providers, avoid NSAIDs; no INR checks or vitamin K limits are needed.

perOption.a: Apixaban wears off quickly; missed doses raise stroke risk.
perOption.b: Apixaban does not need INR monitoring.
perOption.c: Procedures may need planning around the drug.
perOption.d: These are signs of bleeding.
perOption.e: Vitamin K intake does not affect apixaban.
perOption.f: NSAIDs increase bleeding risk; acetaminophen is preferred.

questions.stem: A client with asthma has a new prescription for an inhaled corticosteroid. Which statement shows the client understands how to use it?

options.text: "I'll rinse my mouth with water and spit after each dose."
"I'll use it as soon as I start wheezing during an attack."
"I'll stop using it once I've gone a week without symptoms."
"I'll take it right before my albuterol so it opens my airways."

rationale.correct: Inhaled corticosteroids are daily controllers; rinse and spit after each use, and use a rescue inhaler for acute symptoms.

perOption.a: Rinsing reduces the risk of oral thrush and hoarseness.
perOption.b: Inhaled steroids prevent inflammation; a short-acting bronchodilator is used for attacks.
perOption.c: Controller medicines are taken daily even when symptoms are gone.
perOption.d: The bronchodilator is usually taken first, and the steroid does not open airways quickly.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: A 68-year-old client taking prednisone for COPD is prescribed levofloxacin for pneumonia. On day 3, the client reports sudden pain and swelling above the left heel. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Suggest the client take ibuprofen and walk more to loosen the tight muscle
Tell the client to rest the leg and report the symptoms to the provider today
Explain that this is a common, harmless side effect that will pass in a few days
Tell the client to double the next dose so the infection clears faster

rationale.correct: Fluoroquinolones can cause tendon rupture, especially in people over 60, those taking steroids and transplant recipients; stop activity and report tendon pain.

perOption.a: Walking on a damaged tendon can lead to rupture.
perOption.b: Fluoroquinolones can cause tendinitis and tendon rupture, especially in older adults and those taking steroids; the drug may need to be stopped.
perOption.c: Tendon pain with a fluoroquinolone is serious and needs reporting.
perOption.d: Changing doses is unsafe and does not address the tendon problem.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: A client with Parkinson's disease takes carbidopa-levodopa and says the medicine "wears off" after lunch, when tremors and stiffness return. Lunch is usually a large steak or chicken meal. Which suggestion should the nurse make?

options.text: Take the afternoon dose with the high-protein meal so it is absorbed better
Take the dose about 30 minutes before meals and spread protein over the day
Stop the afternoon dose, since the medicine is not working well enough
Take an extra vitamin B6 supplement at lunch to boost the medication

rationale.correct: Large protein meals reduce levodopa absorption; take doses before meals and spread protein evenly through the day.

perOption.a: Protein competes with levodopa for absorption and can reduce its effect.
perOption.b: Separating doses from large protein meals improves levodopa absorption and reduces wearing-off.
perOption.c: Stopping doses suddenly can worsen symptoms or cause a dangerous reaction.
perOption.d: Vitamin B6 can reduce levodopa's effect.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: A client at 40 weeks is receiving an oxytocin infusion to induce labor. Contractions are now every 1.5 minutes, each lasting 100 seconds, and the fetal heart rate tracing shows late decelerations with each contraction. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Increase the oxytocin rate to bring the baby down faster
Stop the oxytocin infusion
Ask the client to push with the next contraction
Document the tracing and keep watching the next few contractions closely

rationale.correct: With tachysystole and an abnormal fetal heart rate: stop oxytocin, turn the client to the side, give an IV fluid bolus and oxygen as indicated, and notify the provider.

perOption.a: More oxytocin would worsen uterine overstimulation and fetal distress.
perOption.b: Contractions closer than 2 minutes with late decelerations show tachysystole with fetal compromise; stopping oxytocin is the first step.
perOption.c: Pushing is not appropriate unless the cervix is fully dilated, and it does not treat the problem.
perOption.d: Late decelerations with tachysystole need immediate action.

questions.stem: The nurse is admitting a client who is deaf, reads lips and uses American Sign Language. The client's interpreter will arrive in an hour. Which action is best while the nurse explains the admission routine?

options.text: Speak loudly and slowly from the doorway so the client can hear
Face the client in good light, speak clearly at a normal pace and write key points
Ask the client's teenage child to sign for the nurse until the interpreter arrives
Wait until the interpreter arrives in an hour before trying to talk with the client

rationale.correct: For clients who lip-read: face them in good light, speak normally, avoid covering the mouth, write key points and use qualified interpreters for important discussions.

perOption.a: Volume does not help a deaf client, and the doorway is too far for lip reading.
perOption.b: Lip reading needs a clear view of the face; writing confirms important information until the interpreter arrives.
perOption.c: Family members should not interpret medical information, especially children.
perOption.d: The nurse can communicate basic information now by facing the client and writing.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.stem: A client had an above-the-knee amputation 3 days ago. Which position should the nurse encourage to prevent a contracture?

options.text: Lying prone for 20 to 30 minutes several times a day
Keeping a pillow under the residual limb while lying in bed
Sitting in a wheelchair most of the day with the limb resting on a board
Lying on the back with the head of the bed raised to 60 degrees

rationale.correct: After above-the-knee amputation, prevent hip flexion contracture with prone lying, avoid pillows under the limb and limit long periods of sitting.

perOption.a: Prone positioning stretches the hip and prevents a flexion contracture.
perOption.b: A pillow under the limb promotes hip flexion contracture.
perOption.c: Long periods sitting keep the hip flexed.
perOption.d: A high head of bed keeps the hip flexed.

questions.stem: A client recovering from a stroke has a Braden score of 12, is incontinent of urine at times and eats about half of each meal. Which intervention addresses the greatest risk to the client's skin?

options.text: Massage the reddened areas over the sacrum and heels with lotion each shift
Use a pressure-redistributing mattress and reposition the client on a regular schedule
Keep the head of the bed raised to 60 degrees through the day and night to prevent aspiration
Place a disposable incontinence pad under the client in several layers

rationale.correct: A Braden score of 12 means high risk; relieve pressure with support surfaces and repositioning, manage moisture, improve nutrition and avoid shear and massage.

perOption.a: Massaging red bony areas can damage the tissue further.
perOption.b: Pressure is the main cause of pressure injury; redistributing surfaces and turning reduce it.
perOption.c: A high head of bed increases shear on the sacrum.
perOption.d: Multiple layers of pads trap moisture and reduce the effect of the mattress.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.stem: The nurse is giving a client a large-volume cleansing enema before a procedure. Place the steps in order.

items.text: Lubricate the tip of the tubing
Help the client into a left side-lying position with the right knee bent
Raise the container 30 to 45 cm (12 to 18 in) above the anus and let the solution flow slowly
Insert the tip 7.5 to 10 cm (3 to 4 in) into the rectum

rationale.correct: Cleansing enema: left side-lying, lubricate, insert 7.5 to 10 cm in adults and infuse slowly from 30 to 45 cm above the anus.

perOption.a: Left side-lying follows the shape of the colon.
perOption.b: Lubrication eases insertion and prevents injury.
perOption.c: This places the tip past the sphincter in adults.
perOption.d: A slow flow at this height reduces cramping.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.stem: A client with metastatic lung cancer in hospice care asks for the prescribed as-needed morphine for breathlessness. The client's daughter says, "Please don't give so much. I don't want my parent to become an addict." What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "You're right to worry. We'll hold the doses until the breathlessness becomes severe."
"Morphine eases breathlessness, and the goal now is comfort; addiction is not a concern."
"I'll ask the provider to switch your parent to a different medicine that doesn't cause addiction."
"It's your parent's choice, so your worries about addiction don't matter here."

rationale.correct: At the end of life, opioids relieve pain and dyspnea; explain that comfort is the goal and that addiction is not a relevant concern.

perOption.a: Withholding relief causes suffering and is not supported by the risks at the end of life.
perOption.b: Opioids are the main treatment for dyspnea at the end of life; fear of addiction should not prevent comfort.
perOption.c: This reinforces the fear and may lead to less effective relief.
perOption.d: This dismisses the daughter's feelings instead of teaching.

questions.stem: A client newly diagnosed with celiac disease is choosing lunch from the hospital menu. Which choice shows the client understands the diet?

options.text: A turkey sandwich on whole wheat bread with a side of fruit
Grilled chicken with rice, steamed carrots and a baked potato
A bowl of beef and barley soup with a soft bread roll and butter
Spaghetti with meatballs and a slice of garlic toast

rationale.correct: Celiac disease needs a lifelong gluten-free diet: avoid wheat, barley and rye; rice, corn, potatoes, meat, fruit and vegetables are safe.

perOption.a: Wheat contains gluten.
perOption.b: Chicken, rice, vegetables and potatoes are naturally gluten-free.
perOption.c: Barley and bread contain gluten.
perOption.d: Regular pasta, breadcrumbs in meatballs and toast contain gluten.

questions.stem: An 80-year-old client with benign prostatic hyperplasia had hip surgery yesterday. The urinary catheter was removed 8 hours ago. Highlight the findings that suggest urinary retention.

Firm, rounded swelling above the pubic bone

perOption.r1: A large post-void volume shows retention.
perOption.r2: Frequent small voids suggest overflow from a full bladder.
perOption.r3: A distended bladder can be felt above the pubis.

questions.stem: A client recovering from abdominal surgery is anxious and says the pain feels worse at night. The client has received the prescribed analgesic. Which nondrug measure should the nurse offer?

options.text: Guided imagery with slow, deep breathing
A heating pad placed directly over the incision
Walking the hall alone in the dark to tire out the body
Withholding fluids so the client sleeps without waking to void

rationale.correct: Nondrug pain measures such as guided imagery, relaxation breathing, music and positioning work alongside analgesics.

perOption.a: Relaxation and imagery reduce anxiety and the perception of pain alongside medication.
perOption.b: Heat over a fresh incision can increase swelling and bleeding.
perOption.c: Walking alone at night is a fall risk.
perOption.d: Restricting fluids after surgery can cause dehydration.

questions.stem: A client with diabetes and peripheral neuropathy is learning foot care. Which statement shows the client needs more teaching?

options.text: "I'll check my feet each day with a mirror for cuts or blisters."
"I'll soak my feet in hot water each night to soften the skin."
"I'll wear well-fitting shoes and socks, even inside the house."
"I'll have a podiatrist trim my toenails if they get thick or ingrown."

rationale.correct: Diabetic foot care: inspect daily, wash in lukewarm water and dry well, moisturize but not between toes, wear protective shoes and do not soak or self-treat corns.

perOption.a: Daily inspection catches injuries the client may not feel.
perOption.b: Soaking dries and cracks the skin, and hot water can burn feet that cannot feel heat.
perOption.c: Protective footwear prevents injury.
perOption.d: Professional nail care prevents injury.

questions.stem: A client has been on bed rest for 6 days after a pelvic fracture. Which finding should the nurse report to the provider right away?

options.text: Two days without a bowel movement and a mildly firm abdomen
New swelling of the right calf, which measures 3 cm larger than the left
A small area of redness on the sacrum that blanches when pressed
Reduced appetite and saying they feel bored and restless after days of lying in bed

rationale.correct: Immobility raises the risk of DVT, pressure injury, constipation, pneumonia and contractures; new unilateral leg swelling needs prompt reporting.

perOption.a: Constipation is common with immobility and opioids; it needs attention but is not an emergency.
perOption.b: Unilateral calf swelling suggests deep vein thrombosis, which can lead to pulmonary embolism.
perOption.c: Blanchable redness shows pressure but not yet an injury; repositioning is needed.
perOption.d: Boredom and lower appetite are common and are addressed with nursing measures.

questions.stem: A resident with Alzheimer's disease becomes agitated and tries to leave every evening around 1700, saying they must "go home to cook dinner for the children." Which response is most appropriate?

options.text: Remind the resident that their children are grown and that this is now their home
Acknowledge the feeling, talk about the family and offer a calm activity such as folding towels
Give the prescribed as-needed antipsychotic as soon as the resident gets up to leave the unit
Ask the resident to sit in their room alone until they feel calmer and ready to rejoin the group

rationale.correct: For sundowning, validate feelings, redirect to familiar activities, keep routines and lighting steady and avoid arguing or isolation.

perOption.a: Reorienting a resident with moderate dementia often increases distress.
perOption.b: Validating the feeling and redirecting to a familiar task reduce sundowning agitation.
perOption.c: Antipsychotics carry serious risks in dementia and are not the first measure.
perOption.d: Isolation can increase fear and agitation.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old college student of normal weight comes to the clinic for fatigue. Which group of findings most strongly suggests bulimia nervosa?

options.text: BMI of 15, fine body hair, low heart rate and a constant fear of gaining weight
Calluses on the knuckles, swollen cheeks, worn tooth enamel and a potassium of 2.9 mEq/L
Weight gain, eating large amounts when stressed and no purging or other compensation
Tremor, weight loss, heat intolerance, bulging eyes and a fast heart rate at rest

rationale.correct: Bulimia often occurs at normal weight; signs of purging include Russell's sign, parotid swelling, dental erosion and hypokalemia.

perOption.a: Severe underweight, lanugo and bradycardia are more typical of anorexia nervosa.
perOption.b: Knuckle calluses (Russell's sign), parotid swelling, enamel erosion and hypokalemia come from repeated self-induced vomiting.
perOption.c: Binge eating without compensation suggests binge-eating disorder.
perOption.d: These suggest hyperthyroidism.
